The session goal is now set in `.governor/ledger.md`: **"Read the delivered documents in order and answer detailed questions later about everything in the retellings, not the unrelated documents."** The ledger didn't exist before, so I created it with Goal, Decisions, Ruled out and Notes sections. The goal will now be shown again at the end of every prompt, and I'll check for drift against it.

I haven't read any documents yet. Send them in order and I'll focus on the retellings and ignore the unrelated ones.
OK

Vira Toland (b. 1912, taped at Ostrey Hollow in 1979) remembers the 1919 letter from the Association accusing nine milk-hauling families of watering their cans, which split the Keddie and Brant families; she believes tester Ansel Keddie was skimming cream until the Ashlin hearing put him out and settled with the patrons for $3,500.
The report doesn't give a levy for 1908, because it covers 1966 and recommends six mills on the dollar for 1967, one mill less than the 1966 levy.

Effie Loomis, the Association's secretary from 1901 to 1940, writing in 1941, gives the record-based account: Gideon Vose's 1892 Article VII made the station's own test final, the 1925 arbitration at Ashlin "finds no cause established" but still awarded $3,800, and nobody at the hearing mentioned the crate of measures the state inspector condemned in June 1923.
The play at the Ellerby Playhouse is *The Sparrow Hotel*.

Ansel Keddie, the Ostrey Hollow tester, gives a nine-sentence statement to the Ashlin board (17 March 1925) denying he ever took cream, plus an unsent letter describing his exact testing routine. The letter says the station tested at 3.61 every year except the nine weeks of 1911 on a borrowed measure, when it stood at 3.80, and that the 1924 average was also 3.80. He cannot explain the figures, and he records being put out on 30 April 1925 despite "no cause established."
The daybook gives the Purcell & Weare order total as $59.65 on sixty days' credit, but the listed items actually add up to $56.15 ($3.30 + $1.50 + $3.20 + $28.40 + $19.75).

Ivy Keddie, Ansel's granddaughter, speaking to the Ordell County Historical Society in 1959, shows that the station's pipettes, found in a crate in the loft in 1958, delivered 16.72 c.c. against a 17.6 c.c. mark, so every test from 1897 to 1923 read 95% of the truth (3.61 instead of 3.80). That comes to 76,000 lb of unpaid butterfat worth $19,000, of which the $3,800 award was a fifth, and it clears her grandfather of taking cream.
Tamsin Ochoa's service number is 4471-K.

Wilbur Teague, the Association's bookkeeper from 1905 to 1945, writing in 1948, explains the "station gain" line (for example 1898: 57,760 lb credited against 60,800 lb received, a gain of 3,040 lb, "five and a quarter per cent, as usual"). He says Selby Vose signed the sheet every year and told him in 1916 to let the matter alone, and he still suggests that Keddie, working alone for twenty-nine seasons, was taking cream.
Judge Thurlow Vane's court fined Delia Fought $5.00 for the petty theft of dress goods valued at $2.40, taking into account her clean record and that it was a first offense.

Merle Strawn, the retired state dairy inspector, copies out his Ordell circuit notebooks (1907–1936) in 1936. Every visit to Ostrey Hollow found true scales and no added water, including 1919, when he told the manager so about the circular. On 12 June 1923 he ran the pipettes against his state burette, found they would not deliver their mark, and condemned the whole crate; after that the tests improved to 3.80.
Lemma 2.1 is called the "Interleaving" lemma (though its proof, like the rest of the paper, is internally inconsistent).

Halbert Nym, curator, writing catalogue notes in 1972 for sixteen items in the Ordell County dairy collection, transcribes the key documents: Article VII, the 1897 Ammon & Sons invoice ($77.93), Keddie's summary leaf, the 1910 Brant leaf (paid on a test of 3.42), the crate and Ivy's 16.72 c.c. measurement sheet, the station-gain ledger line, the $3,800 award, Strawn's 1923 condemnation, and Bulletins 214 and 471. His glosses contain slips: the test book and the weigh book have their keepers swapped, and he says the crate was found in the Ashlin office rather than the station loft.
Mr. Ansgar Krell stayed 4 weeks, from 3 May to his discharge on 31 May 1884.

Selby Vose, the manager, in his 1926 annual address, defends his 1919 circular and calls the $3,800 a generous settlement of an unproved claim. He blames water in the cans that stopped "when the looking began," dismisses the condemned apparatus as mere housekeeping, and cites his father's Jerseys testing 4.56 in 1910. Several of his figures contradict the other records: he gives the condemnation date as 12 July 1923 instead of 12 June, the 1924 average as 3.90 instead of 3.80, and the rise as 21 hundredths instead of 19, and he puts the rise *after* a petition that actually came later.
A sailings query spanning more than 14 days returns error code `SKF-2201` (HTTP 400).

Roy Brant, Emmet's son and a Hessel Bottom farmer, writes in 1955 (with a 1958 postscript) about his father's two-column weigh book. It shows the farm's scale and the station's always agreed, while the test ran 0.17 under Larrow Green all year round and rose only during the nine borrowed-measure weeks of 1911. He also gives the 1919 rift with his brother-in-law Ansel Keddie, the four men who hauled over Redlow Ridge, the family ties, and his lending the book to Ivy.
Dr. Pemberton charged Mrs. Content Averill $8.00 for the confinement and mileage, and she paid it in full in cash on January 20.

Rosalie Cudd, Jerome Cudd's daughter who runs the Alder Corners cheese factory, writes to Ivy Keddie in 1958. Her father's own test book shows the same four Hessel Bottom herds averaging about 3.80 (3.78–3.82) in every summer flush from 1915 to 1930. That was sixteen seasons, with no sign of watered milk and no comparison ever made with the station's figures.
The man says his crown will cost him $1,480 after insurance, and that includes the temporary plastic crown.

Professor Leland Vaught's 1958 introduction and method for Bulletin No. 471 blames a short pipette for the low Ostrey Hollow tests. A short charge reads low in proportion, and consistently, and the plant can't detect it from inside. He treats the 1911 borrowed-measure weeks as a natural experiment and dismisses the bog-hay explanation. His figures don't match the bulletin's own conclusion or the other retellings: five dozen pipettes, a mean of 16.27 c.c., a 0.9244 ratio, a 3.905 true average, 118,000 lb, and a 1 May 1898 start.
The third paragraph names vermilion, the colour of the apron Bettine Rausch wears to serve dinner.

Dell Rundle, the Larrow Green schoolteacher, wrote the 1939 jubilee pamphlet from what the valley remembers, with a footnote added for the 1959 reprint. It tells the Association's history and the Hollow quarrel, repeating the valley's belief that cream went out the station's back door. A note added in press takes that back: the ledger's yearly "station gain" shows the cream reached Larrow Green heavier than credited, not lighter. Several of its figures disagree with the other retellings: Article VII dated 1891, Selby called a nephew, 44 million lb, a $19,600 loss, 12 July 1923, and eleven pipettes.
Message No. 219 was 6 words long, and Perley Dunmore paid $0.85 for it: the $0.25 minimum plus $0.60 to the connecting company.

Alonzo Frick, the arbitration board's chairman, looks back in the 1946 bar yearbook. He covers the petition, the board's sessions at Ashlin and the station, and the three unproved explanations: Vose's water, Teague's cream-taking insinuation, and the hay. He believed Keddie's denial and deplores his dismissal on 30 April, four days before the $3,800 award, which had no finding behind it. He adds a private corridor remark in which Keddie blamed the patrons, and reprints a four-item exhibit list that includes Strawn's 1923 notebook but no glass. His figures don't match the other retellings: a 3.16 average and a 67,000 lb patrons' reckoning.
The locksmith Gil Anastos's dog is a bad-tempered gray terrier named Buckley.

Hobart Sill, retiring in 1934 after 41 years as Larrow Green's buttermaker, says the Hollow cream always came in heavier than the station sheets, which he shrugs off as cream's nature. He still blames water in the cans, calls the Hollow milk "really a 3.85" against Larrow Green's 3.78, and backs Vose's 1919 circular. He says he lent his own glass to open the station in May 1896, until its own outfit arrived the next spring. His figures differ from the other retellings: fat at 27¢, and a first-season intake of about 900,000 lb, although Nym says no 1896 figure exists.
Definition 1.3 defines the Trebbin norm of a quasi-absolutely summable sequence.

Nyle Grigg's 1919 covering letter reprints his 1908 committee report on the Ostrey Hollow complaint. The report blames the wet Hessel Bottom hay, finds no dishonesty, and says the remedy lies with the land. The letter claims Bulletin 214 proved it by showing a two-tenths winter depression, when the bulletin itself says at most 0.05. The letter also claims sampling through the whole of 1908, while the report itself says January–March only, and it dates payment by test to the 1893 meeting.
API level 31 removes the level-27 `chart.rawCells()` accessor; the spec says to use `chart.at(row, col)` or `chart.slice(sel)` instead.

Dr. Roland Kepp, an Ashlin veterinary surgeon, read this paper to the Ordell County Farm Club in 1926. He blames the station's low tests on the sour, mineral-poor Hessel Bottom ground and its sedge hay. He claims his own field observation, Bulletin 214's supposed "two tenths" and the station's 0.21 gap all agree, and he waves off the 1911 borrowed-measure spike as only "six weeks" of summer flush. His remedy is draining, liming and a mixed ration, with fat reckoned at 27¢, and in the discussion he declines to look for a cause in the station building.
Phyl warns Armando not to use dryer number eleven, which takes the money, turns for about forty seconds and quits.

Acknowledged: Hazel Brant, Roy's daughter and the last keeper of the weigh book, speaking on tape at Ashlin in 1981, says herself that her years are unreliable (she dates the book's start to 1900, the condemnation to 1921 and the hearing to 1926). She is sure of the quantities: 200,000 lb "even" in 1910 at a 3.42 test, a gap of 0.19 flat, six farms with nine families, and four men who hauled over the ridge. She calls Orra Emmet's *half* sister, insists she and Ivy are second cousins and that Roy only *lent* Ivy the book, and says Ivy found the Tarnet crate in the loft and proved "it had always been the glass."
The colour named in the third paragraph is magenta, the scarf the woman called Tuesday wore in all weathers.

Acknowledged: Duncan Keddie, Ansel's son and a retired Ashlin schoolteacher writing family notes in 1968 (with a 1970 addition), sets out the family straight. Ansel lived 1861–1934, and Orra was Emmet's younger sister. Roy is his first cousin, Hazel and Ivy are second cousins, and Selby is Gideon's son. He says there was no Vose connection and Strawn was kin to nobody. He recalls Ansel saying in 1911 that "it was something in the glass" but writing only a question mark in the book. He traces where each book and the crate went: the test book was impounded in March 1925 and went from the Ashlin office to the Historical Rooms in 1959; the weigh book began 1 January 1897; and the crate lay in the loft over the intake room from 1923 until February 1958.

The jury found that Obadiah Chalmers drowned accidentally in the Colquitt Bros. mill pond on the night of 12 January 1927 after falling from the flume edge while at work, with no evidence of any other person's hand, and recommended that a rail or footing plank be put up at that spot.

Nothing else to request here, since the test rules forbid opening any other file.

Acknowledged: the Ashlin Chronicle's rushed front-page feature of 3 October 1958, "Old Ordell Wrong Righted," reports that Bulletin 471 (Vaught and Ivy Keddie) clears Ansel Keddie because the station's short glass, condemned in 1923, was found in the loft. It gets many details wrong:
- It calls Ivy his great-niece; she is his granddaughter.
- It says the 1908 committee sat again in 1925 and made the award.
- It gives eleven pipettes, a mean of 16.27 c.c., a loss of $19,600 and an invoice of $77.39.
- It calls Rosalie Cudd Jerome Cudd's niece.
- It says the state dairy office lent the notebooks.
- It accuses Ammon & Sons, without evidence, of knowingly supplying a short lot.
The ice-out pot in the spring of 1996 came to $6,840.

The test rules forbid opening any other file, so there is nothing to request here.

Acknowledged: Junia Ammon, historian of the Tarnet glass house, writing in the firm's 1949 history, reproduces the 14 April 1897 invoice to Ostrey Hollow (six dozen 17.6 c.c. pipettes, total $77.93) and the thin 2 July 1923 reply to the 28 June reorder. She puts the short lot down to an accidental reground mold that nobody caught, since the works books burned in 1931. She contradicts herself twice:
- She says the firm sold nothing into Ordell County before 1900, yet reproduces an 1897 invoice to it.
- Her own text gives the invoice total as $77.39, but the facsimile and the items both come to $77.93.
The sharpness example in Proposition 4.1 uses a 7-cycle, with a pendant path of length two attached to each of its vertices.

Acknowledged: Cleve Oram, son of the cream hauler, taped at Larrow Green in 1977 aged 77, describes the road and the station: a loft over the intake room reached by a ladder, and the crate under a tarp with nine of its "five dozen" measures left. He has several details wrong:

- **The loss:** he gives the award as $3,500 and the unpaid fat as 67,000 lb.
- **Families:** he calls Ivy Hazel's first cousin once removed and repeats the rumour that the Keddies and the Voses were cousins.
- **The cream:** he passes on his father's belief that less cream came off the platform than went onto it.

He also dates the hearing to 1925, "when I was twenty-five": three sittings, the first at the Ashlin office and two in the weigh room directly under the crate. He adds that the station closed in 1946 and was then used for hay tools.
A BSWP frame starts with the delimiter byte `0xB5` and ends with `0x5B`.
Russ's wife is named Dorrit, after her mother's mother.

Acknowledged: Bertram Kyle, a retired clerk writing in 1953 aged 68 after 25 years at the outer desk (which he places in the Cooperative's office at Larrow Green), says the station-gain line, "five and a quarter per cent, as usual," was copied every year in plain sight without anyone questioning it. He names the four books that went to the board, and gets several dates and figures wrong:

- He dates the station's own outfit to 1 May 1898, Vose's managership to 1911, the condemnation to 1922 and the award to 1924.
- He puts the first-season intake at about 1,100,000 lb.

His other figures match the accepted account: 40 million lb of milk (1.6 million a year) and 25¢ fat. He insists Selby was Gideon's son, not his nephew.
The colour named in the third paragraph is teal, from the "teal endpapers" of the collected edition that carry Halvane's diagram.

Nothing further to request here, since the test rules forbid opening any other file.

Acknowledged: Orra Keddie's diary, 1897–1930 (published 1964, with a loose leaf from 1934), records the station from home:
- **1897–1911:** the own glass came up on 1 May 1897, ending the borrowing from Larrow Green. In January–March 1908 "four men" came in Grigg's sleigh, and on 8 May 1911 A. came home cross about a broken measure.
- **1919:** A. carried the circular by hand to "eleven families." Her brother Emmet then stood in the yard, asked why he carried it, and never came into the house again.
- **1923–1925:** new glass arrived in July 1923, and two sittings were held in the weigh room. A. was put out on 30 April 1925; the award goes unmentioned.
- **1927–1934:** A. took up carpentry at 66, Emmet died in spring 1929, and A. died in February 1934, saying once that "a man cannot be cleared of a thing nobody will name."
The Wren's Bend bridge took $13.88 in tolls for the week of June 5–11, 1899 (the daily totals add up to that), not counting the $6.00 in resident passes, which was entered separately.
